BOOK_A.title: Application for Judgment Against Defendant Noted in Default
BOOK_A.operative_text_raw:
3.37(1)The plaintiff may,without notice to any other party, on proof of the*plaintiff's claim,apply to the Court for judgment in respect of a claim for which*default judgment has not been entered if
*(a)one or more defendants are noted in default,or*(b)the defendant's statement of defence is struck out.*(2)In the circumstances described in subrule (1) the plaintiff is entitled to a*costs award.*(3)The Court may do one or more of the following:*(a)pronounce judgment;
*(b)make any necessary order;*(c)direct a determination of damages;*(d)adjourn the application and order additional evidence to be provided;*(f)direct that the claim proceed to trial and that notice be served on*every other defendant;*(g)make a costs award in favour of the plaintiff.

BOOK_A.commentary:
How does a plaintiff get to judgment if a defendant does not file or serve a statement of defence and part or all of the claim against him is unliquidated, e.g., damages? Of course the matter can just be sent to"assessment" in the usual way:a trial with live evidence by a judge on issues of quantum (not liability).That is R.3.37(3)(c), and is really just inherent in the court's usual procedure.But R.3.37 gives alternative simpler procedures which can be used if the amounts

are smaller, or if the matter is not very contentious.For example, sometimes a claim technically is unliquidated, but there is not much doubt how to compute it. If pleadings of the defendant are struck out, the plaintiff cannot enter a money judgment in an unliquidated case without proof of amount, and instead should go to assessment. Very often the loss sustained can be assessed from affidavits, without live evidence.

For constitutional and statutory reasons, whether an Applications Judge can assess damages is now unsettled. However, in some cases of disputed facts, it might be more efficient for a justice to order a reference to an Applications Judge to take evidence and report back on damages, to be confirmed by a judge.

If part of the suit is for a liquidated claim and part is for an unliquidated claim, the plaintiff should be able to sign judgment for the liquidated part and have the rest reserved and put down for assessment. Where a statement of claim claims two alternative remedies, though the defendant is noted in default, he should be given notice of a motion to pick one remedy.Default admits liability, but not

which remedy, especially if legal issues are involved. A judgment by one judge under R.3.37, after noting all the defendants in default, without live evidence, and no evidence at all as regards one defendant, and affidavit evidence re the other defendants, may be a judgment by default.If so, the Rules let another judge set it aside.

A defendant noted in default cannot raise a limitations defence, because it has to be pled, despite R.3.37.

BOOK_B.title: Application for judgment against defendant noted in default

commentary.text: Rule 3.37 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.37. 1. Deemed Admission of Facts; Cause of Action Must Still Be Established In Toerper v. Hoard, 2011 ABQB 85, 2011 CarswellAlta 194, the defendant's Statement of Defence had been previously struck out. An application for judgment then came before Madam Justice Strekaf. Her Ladyship said that the defendant was deemed to have admitted the facts alleged in the Statement of Claim. At paragraphs 2–4, Strekaf, J. said: 2 Rule 3.37 of the new Rules of Court provides for an application to the court for judgment where a defendant has been noted in default or where the defendant's Statement of Defence is struck out. 3 The purpose of an assessment of damages is to determine the quantum of damages, rather than the liability for damages, provided that the facts deemed to have been admitted establish the cause of action. A defendant who is noted in default is deemed to have admitted the allegations of fact contained in the Statement of Claim. 4 This issue was addressed in the context of the predecessor provision to Rule 3.37 in the old Rules of Court in Robinson v. Fiesta Hotel Group Resorts, 2008 ABQB 311, 450 A.R. 167, where Yamauchi J. stated at paragraphs 10–12: [10] The strongest statement on the effect of the Defendants' failure to file a statement of defence was made by the Supreme Court of Canada in McElroy v. Cowper-Smith, [1967] S.C.R. 425 at 428, where Spence J., considered the reasoning in Sulef v. Parkin (1966), 57 W.W.R. (N.S.) 236 (Alta. C.A.), and said: … in the province of Alberta upon default in defence the defendant is to be taken to have admitted the facts set out in the statement of claim. This is a decision of the highest court in Alberta on a point of practice in the province, and this court will not interfere under such circumstances. Therefore, the Defendant, as plaintiffs at trial, were not required to prove publication of the alleged libel. [11] Although Spence, J., was writing in dissent, many Alberta cases since that time have held that the effect of a noting in default is that the defendant has admitted the facts alleged in the statement of claim by the failure to deny them, see e.g. Klinck v. Drinnan, [1985] A.J. No. 576; 66 A.R. 321 (Q.B.), Dykes v. Goczan, [1996] A.J. No. 432; 188 A.R. 352 (Q.B.) (“Dykes”); Syncrude Canada Ltd. v. Tibo Steel Products Ltd. et al., [2001] A. J. No. 736; 292 A.R. 368; 2001 ABQB 478; Dyck et al v. Wilkinson et al., [2004] A.R. Uned. 657; [2004] A.J. No. 1155; 2004 ABQB 731. More relevant to the case with which this Court is dealing is a statement by Harvey, C.J.A. in Brennan v. Arcadia Coal Co. (1929), 24 Alta. L.R. 236 (C.A.), at 448 (“Brennan”), where he said: The amount of damages to which the plaintiff was entitled could only be ascertained by an assessment but the evidence to be taken on such assessment would only be for the purpose of ascertaining the amount of, and in no sense the liability for, such damages which latter has been established by the facts alleged, and admitted by the Defendant by reason of its failure to deny them. [12] The mere noting in default, however, does not end the matter. In Dykes at para. 6, Binder J., based on Spiller v. Brown, [1973] 6 W.W.R. 663 (Alta. C.A.) (“Spiller”), said that there is an exception to the rule that the Defendant has admitted the facts alleged in the statement of claim by failure to deny them “where the Court is not satisfied that the Plaintiff has a cause of action, the Court has a duty to direct a hearing to determine the matter.” This Court has reviewed the pleadings filed in this matter and has heard the testimony of Robinson and concludes that the Plaintiffs have a cause of action against the Defendants. In Boyer v. Boyer, 2024 ABKB 727, the defendant's pleadings were struck out as a contempt sanction. The question arose as to what extent the defendant could then participate in the subsequent trial. Justice Lema said: [52] Most of the no-defendant cases involve defendants noted in default, versus struck-pleadings defendants. [53] I find that the principles governing noting-in-default cases apply equally to those involving struck pleadings. [54] In both scenarios, the defendant has, or ends up with, no pleading in opposition to the statement of claim. [55] In the struck-pleadings scenario, the defendant ends up in the same position as if he, she or it had not defended in the first place. [56] Technically speaking, the plaintiff in a struck-pleadings scenario could note the defendant in default post-striking; however, that step appears unnecessary, with the striking accomplishing the same thing (no defence, or no more defence). [57] As I see it, the functional equivalence of the two scenarios is recognized in Rules 3.36 and 3.37, which provide the same consequences and next-step options for the Court and the parties i.e. whether no defence was filed or a defence was struck. … [62] The critical impact of a noting in default or pleading being struck is losing the ability to challenge the facts asserted in the opposing party's pleadings…. … [86] The admissions implied from a noting in default or defence striking do not extend to statement-of-claim positions on questions of law or questions of mixed fact and law. … [94] To this point, I have concluded that, because of the striking, Mr. Boyer is deemed to have admitted the factual allegations in Ms. Boyer's statement of claim. And that he cannot introduce evidence contradicting those allegations. [95] Can he introduce other (not-contradicting) evidence? Submit a brief? Make opening and closing statements? Cross-examine the plaintiff and her witness(es)? Take other steps? … [97] Rule 3.37(1) contemplates, at least in some circumstances, the plaintiff proceeding, and the court deciding, without notice to a struck or noted-in-default defendant. [98] I do not read that as necessarily translating to a bar on such a defendant participating e.g. where notice is given and the defendant wishes to participate. … [101] As noted earlier, no Alberta rule expressly bars a struck-pleadings defendant from participating in the trial of the matter i.e. where the plaintiff has notified the defendant of the trial and the defendant wishes to participate. … Justice Lema then reviewed several Alberta cases, and on the issue of whether a party whose pleadings have been struck can participate in the trial, said: [120] The cases featuring participation square better (i.e. than the no-participation cases) with the flexibility accorded by Rule 3.37(3), especially Rule 3.37(3)(b) (“make any necessary order”). [121] The “make any necessary order” power is sufficiently broad to authorize participation by a struck or noted-in-default defendant and to set its bounds. … [127] …I find that the Court has sufficient power under Rule 3.37(3)(b) (“make any necessary order”) to allow a struck or noted-in-default party to give evidence i.e. as long as it does not contradict any of the deemed-admitted facts in the plaintiff's claim, subject to considering the reason(s) for pleadings being struck (as here), as discussed further below. … [130] As I see it, Rule 3.37(3) – in particular, its “make any necessary order” element — allows the Court, in appropriate circumstances, to permit defined participation by a noted-in-default or struck-pleadings defendant. [131] Participation may be warranted where it promotes the fundamental purpose of the Rules i.e. “provid[ing] a means by which claims can be fairly and justly resolved in or by a court process in a timely and cost-effective way” (Rule 1.2(1)). Particularly where the benefits of allowing participation, including “provid[ing] the court with a richer record on which to base its decision” and “allow[ing] for a fair [or fairer] adjudication of the issues” (per Mullin v Sherlock, 2018 ONCA 1063 (para 55)), outweigh the costs, including possible delays e.g. where a scheduled trial, built on one-party participation, might have to be pushed back to accommodate two-party steps. In TLA Food Services Ltd. v. 1144707 Alberta Ltd., 2011 ABQB 550, 2011 CarswellAlta 1540, 525 A.R. 1, 56 Alta. L.R. (5th) 363, Justice Shelley discussed the effect of noting a defendant in default. At paragraphs 18 and 24, Shelly, J. summarized the law: 18 Strekaf J., in Toerper v. Hoard, 2011 ABQB 85, discussed the effect of a defendant's failure to file a defence under R. 3.37, citing Robinson v. Fiesta Hotel Group Resorts, 2008 ABQB 311, 450 AR 167 and McElroy v. Cowper-Smith, [1967] S.C.R. 425. These cases, and others cited therein, provide that under the old rules (Alta Reg 390/1968), in Alberta noting in default means that the facts alleged in the Statement of Claim are admitted by the defendant. (Robinson at para. 11; McElroy at p. 425 (per Hall J.) and 428 (per Spence J.). Strekaf J. applied these principles to the new Rule. I agree that these principles continue to apply. … 24 A summary of these principles follows: 1. When a defendant is noted in default, it is deemed to have admitted the allegations in the Statement of Claim; 2. Before granting default judgment the Court must still inquire as to whether a cause of action is made out in the Statement of Claim, and may direct a hearing on the matter; 3. A defendant who has been noted in default cannot adduce evidence to contradict the facts alleged in the Statement of Claim in the course of a hearing for the assessment of damages; 4. Quantum of damages may be assessed based on affidavit evidence; 5. R. 152 of the previous rules gives the Chambers judge discretion as to whether to grant default judgment ex parte based on affidavit evidence or to require that notice be given and an assessment set down for hearing. In Argent v. Gray, 2015 ABQB 292, a defendant had been noted in default. However, he would have had a defence under the Limitations Act. Justice Dario concluded that the defendant could not avail himself of that defence though the Plaintiff could still be required to prove its claim against the defendant: 44 Having been noted in default, Mr. McMillan cannot avail himself of the limitations defence applicable to the other Defendants. In Makowichuk v Makowichuk, 2013 ABCA 439, 60 CPC (7th) 448 at para 9, the Court of Appeal held: • The appellant's position is of course contrary to s 3 of the Limitations Act, the relevant portion of which provides: “the defendant on pleading this Act as a defence, is entitled to immunity from liability in respect of the claim.” In other words, it requires that the defence be pleaded in order to give rise to the immunity. The logical extension of the appellant's position is that the immunity is available without so pleading, indeed, without even filing the Statement of Defence. In our opinion, that position is without merit. 45 Nevertheless, given that Rule 3.37 allows a court to dismiss a plaintiff's claim notwithstanding a noting in default, I am satisfied that the Plaintiffs cannot succeed against Mr. McMillan unless they prove their claim against him …. 2. Service of Amended Statement of Claim when Defendant Noted in Fault In Clarke v. Deranger, 2006 ABQB 442, 2006 CarswellAlta 773, 400 A.R. 327, 64 Alta. L.R. (4th) 382, Macklin J. stated, at p. 334: 30 While Rule 144 of the Rules of Court does provide that a defendant “who fails to defend or demand notice is not entitled to notice of any subsequent proceedings in the action,” this can only refer to proceedings that relate to the allegations in the original statement of claim of which the defendant has either received, or been deemed to have received, notice. I am not prepared to interpret the Rule as having the effect of allowing a plaintiff to proceed against a defendant on new allegations of which the defendant has no knowledge when the defendant has been noted in default of filing a defence to the original statement of claim. 31 A defendant who is served, either personally or substitutionally, with a copy of a statement of claim, may decide not to defend the action because the allegations are true, they are insufficient to make out a case against the defendant, or for some other reason. However, the defendant's failure to file a defence to a statement of claim does not give the plaintiff carte blanche to amend the claim by adding serious allegations against the defendant which will expose him to liability, where he did not have any before, or increase his potential liability, and then to proceed as though the defendant has admitted those new allegations. 3. When the Court Doubts There Is a Cause of Action In Dykes v. Goczan (1996), 38 Alta. L.R. (3d) 425 (Q.B.), the defendant had been noted in default but sought leave to tender evidence contradicting the facts set forth in the Statement of Claim. Binder J. dismissed the application, but agreed that leave could be granted if the Court were of the view that the plaintiff did not have a cause of action. At pp. 353-354, His Lordship said: …[W]hen a defendant is noted in default the legal position in Alberta is that the defendant has admitted the facts alleged in the Statement of Claim by the failure to deny them. There is, however, an exception, which is the basis of the Spiller[Spiller v. Brown, [1973] 6 W.W.R. 663 (Alta. C.A.)] decision, that where the court is not satisfied that the plaintiff has a cause of action, the court has a duty to direct a hearing to determine the matter. In that case for example, the trial judge had a suspicion that the plaintiff was manoeuvring to remove other defendants from the action to avoid the need to prove that the defendant who had not filed a defence was guilty of gross negligence. 4. When Alternative Remedies Were Sought In TLA Food Services Ltd. v. 1144707 Alberta Ltd., 2011 ABQB 550, 2011 CarswellAlta 1540, 525 A.R. 1, 56 Alta. L.R. (5th) 363, a Plaintiff noted a Defendant in default. The Statement of Claim sought damages, rectification of the contract in dispute, and specific performance of the contract. Justice Shelley held that the Defendant was entitled to notice of which remedy the Plaintiff sought, and that an ex parte application for rectification was not appropriate. At paragraphs 53-54, her Ladyship said: 53 In Fenske v. Schneider, 2007 ABQB 164, Veit J. held that, where a plaintiff has sought alternative remedies, the defendant should be given notice of a motion by the plaintiff to seek one of those remedies. Veit J. noted “a default of defence is an admission of the facts pleaded, not of the conclusions of law or the assessment of damages” (at para. 11) and “that the appropriate remedy flowing from that breach is not a fact which [the defendant] can be taken to have admitted” (at para. 15). In Fenske the plaintiff sought either damages or specific performance in the Statement of Claim, and then sought specific performance in the application for default judgment. Veit J. refused the application, noting (at paras. 15-16): … not only does the Statement of Claim itself advances two possible remedies, the remedy of specific performance is a discretionary, equitable remedy which will only be granted after a review of all pertinent circumstances. Mr. Fenske may well have a strong claim for specific performance: Fossum, [1997] A.J. No. 1255, Holden, [2002] A.J. No. 1424, United Gulf Developments Ltd., [2004] N.S.J. No. 66, Spicer, [2005] A.J. No. 1074. That is not the point. The issue is that Ms. Schneider may well have a position concerning the request for specific performance as opposed to a request for damages; she is entitled to advance that position for the court's consideration. 54 Similarly here, TLA's Claim sought damages, rectification of the Contract, and specific performance. In my view, as in Fenske, notice must be given to the Defendants of TLA's choice of remedy so that they can advance a position in regards to the appropriate equitable remedy. I conclude that this is a further ground for denying TLA's application. 5. Effects of Noting in default or Striking of defence In Boyer v. Boyer, 2024 ABKB 727, Justice Lema discussed the possible effects of having a defence struck, or being noted in default: [52] Most of the no-defendant cases involve defendants noted in default, versus struck-pleadings defendants. [53] I find that the principles governing noting-in-default cases apply equally to those involving struck pleadings. [54] In both scenarios, the defendant has, or ends up with, no pleading in opposition to the statement of claim. [55] In the struck-pleadings scenario, the defendant ends up in the same position as if he, she or it had not defended in the first place. [56] Technically speaking, the plaintiff in a struck-pleadings scenario could note the defendant in default post-striking; however, that step appears unnecessary, with the striking accomplishing the same thing (no defence, or no more defence). [57] As I see it, the functional equivalence of the two scenarios is recognized in Rules 3.36 and 3.37, which provide the same consequences and next-step options for the Court and the parties i.e. whether no defence was filed or a defence was struck. … [62] The critical impact of a noting in default or pleading being struck is losing the ability to challenge the facts asserted in the opposing party's pleadings, as explained in the cases below, starting with Robinson v Fiesta Hotel Group Resorts, 2008 ABQB 311 (Yamauchi J.): The strongest statement on the effect of the Defendants' failure to file a statement of defence was made by the Supreme Court of Canada in McElroy v. Cowper-Smith, 1967 CanLII 70 (SCC), [1967] S.C.R. 425 at 428, where Spence J. considered the reasoning in Sulef v. Parkin (1966), 1966 CanLII 638 (AB CA), 57 W.W.R. 236 (Alta. S.C.- App. Div.) and said: … in the province of Alberta upon default in defence the defendant is to be taken to have admitted the facts set out in the statement of claim. This is a decision of the highest court in Alberta on a point of practice in the province, and this court will not interfere under such circumstances. Therefore, the respondents, as plaintiffs at trial, were not required to prove publication of the alleged libel. Although Spence J. was writing in dissent, many Alberta cases since that time have held that the effect of a noting in default is that the defendant has admitted the facts alleged in the statement of claim by the failure to deny them, see e.g. Klinck v. Drinnan, [1985] A.J. No. 576 (Q.B.), Dykes v. Goczan, [1996] A.J. No. 432 (Q.B.) (“Dykes”); Syncrude Canada Ltd. v. Tibo Steel Products Ltd., 2001 ABQB 478 (CanLII), [2001] A. J. No. 736 (Q.B.); Dyck v. Wilkinson, 2004 ABQB 731 (CanLII), [2004] A. J. No. 1155 (Q.B.). More relevant to the case with which this Court is dealing is a statement by Harvey C.J.A. in Brennan v. Arcadia Coal Co. (1929), 1929 CanLII 274 (AB CA), 24 Alta. L.R. 236 at 448 (C.A.) (“Brennan”), where he said: The amount of damages to which the plaintiff was entitled could only be ascertained by an assessment but the evidence to be taken on such assessment would only be for the purpose of ascertaining the amount of, and in no sense the liability for, such damages which latter has been established by the facts alleged and admitted by the defendant by reason of its failure to deny them. [paras 10-11] [emphasis added] [63] As Yamauchi J. discussed further, the court must be satisfied that the admitted facts add up to a cause of action and that it has jurisdiction to grant the requested relief: The mere noting in default, however, does not end the matter. In Dykes at para. 6, Binder J., based on Spiller v. Brown, 1973 ALTASCAD 76 (CanLII), [1973] 6 W.W.R. 663 (Alta. C.A.) (“Spiller”), said that there is an exception to the rule that the defendant has admitted the facts alleged in the statement of claim by failure to deny them “where the Court is not satisfied that the Plaintiff has a cause of action, the Court has a duty to direct a hearing to determine the matter.” This Court has reviewed the pleadings filed in this matter and has heard the testimony of Robinson and concludes that the Plaintiffs have a cause of action against the Defendants. Plaintiffs' counsel argued that the pleadings, proof of service of the pleadings on the Defendants and the praecipe to note in default all provide this Court with jurisdiction to assess damages. This Court disagrees with that proposition based on the statement by Johnson J.A. in Spiller at para. 8, where he said, “Neither by pleadings nor admissions can a defendant give a court jurisdiction that it does not otherwise have,” see also Muscutt v. Courcelles (2002), 2002 CanLII 44957 (ON CA), 213 D.L.R. (4th) 577, 160 O.A.C. 1, 60 O.R. (3rd) 20, 13 C.C.L.T. (3rd) 161, 26 C.P.C. (5th) 206 at para. 50 (Ont. C.A.) (“Muscutt”). Thus, this Court must determine whether it has jurisdiction even in the face of the noting in default. [paras 12-13] [emphasis added] [64] As confirmed in Smith v Tuchscherer, 2024 ABCA 186: … when proceeding on default or after pleadings are struck, counsel and parties remain obliged to prove entitlement to the remedies sought and to respect the limits of the served pleadings: TLA Food Services Ltd v 1144707 Alberta Ltd, 2011 ABQB 550 [Shelley J.]. [65] Another dimension of participation is applying for relief under the Rules of Court. In the analogous context of a party being noted in default, the noted-in-default party is still a party for the purpose of “tak[ing] any other step under the Rules”, per Yaremchuk v Haight, 2001 ABCA 7 (considering the pre-2010 Rules): In my view, a party who is noted in default does not cease to be a party to the action and is entitled to utilize Rule 244.1 [dismissal-for-delay rule]. According to Rule 142(3) once a defendant has been noted in default he or she is no longer entitled to deliver a statement of defence or demand of notice. Furthermore, once the defendant has been noted in default: [a]ll the plaintiff has to prove, or the defendant is permitted to controvert, is the amount of the damages; for the cause of action itself, as stated in the plaintiff's claim, and the right to some damages in respect of it, is admitted by the defendant, by his suffering judgement to pass against him by default. T.W. Chitty, ed., Chitty's Archibold's Practice of the Queen's Bench Division, vol. 2, 14th ed. (London: Sweet & Maxwell, 1885) at 1336, as cited in Sulef v. Parkin and Breno (1966), 1966 CanLII 638 (AB CA), 57 W.W.R. 236 (Alta. C.A.) But I have not been provided with any authority or directed to any Rule which might otherwise limit the right of a defendant to take any other step under the Rules. [para 5] [emphasis added] [66] A noted-in-default party's participation rights (there too to apply to have the remaining party's action struck for delay) were again examined in Zivkovic v Zivkovic, 2009 ABQB 542 (Veit J.). [67] Zivkovic was decided under the former rules but with an awareness of the proposed new (circa 2010) rules, including Rules 3.36 and 3.37. [68] After considering Yaremchuk (cited above), Veit J. observed: The approach taken by our Court of Appeal is not the approach taken in other jurisdictions. For example, the Ontario Rules of Court specifically state that a defendant who is in default cannot ask for dismissal of an action for delay: see Rule 24.01. However, in Ontario, a defendant who is in default can apply to the court for leave to bring a motion other than a motion to set the default praecipe aside. While that approach may be more logically consistent, our Court of Appeal has effectively short-circuited the need to make an application to move under R. 244.1 [dismissal for long delay]. [para 31] [emphasis added] [69] She concluded: It appears to me that ALRI's proposed new Rules of Court [i.e. which became the 2010 Rules] do not clarify the issues raised by this motion [i.e. a noted-in-default party's rights]: proposed Rules 3.36(1)(b), R. 3.37(1)(a), [and] R. 4.33 do not appear to give more guidance that is present under the existing Rules. Given the increasing number of self-represented litigants, especially in family law matters, it might be useful to provide explicit direction to such litigants about, for example, the effect of not defending an action. [para 37] [emphasis added] [70] I echo Veit J.s comments, finding them equally applicable to a struck-pleadings scenario. In both scenarios, the 2010 Rules do not explicitly address the effect of a party being noted in default or having its pleadings struck. While Rules 3.36 and 3.37 (discussed further below) provide various options for the Court in such scenarios, they do not (or at least not expressly) address whether the defendant continues to have any right(s) to participate in the proceeding or, if so, the nature and extent of any such right(s). … [73] On another dimension of participation, a noted-in-default or struck-pleadings party continues to be entitled to copies of orders and judgments affecting them, per Rule 9.8: Unless these rules otherwise provide or the Court otherwise orders, the party who enters the judgment or order must serve a copy of the entered judgment or order on each of the other parties. [74] The core definition of “party” (Appendix to the Rules of Court) is “a party to an action.” Per Yaremchuk (cited above), a noted-in-default (or, by extension, struck-pleadings) litigant does not cease to be a party (para 5). [75] On the overall impacts of pleadings being struck, Shelley J. surveyed the Alberta noting-in-default case law (which I find applicable to the struck-pleadings scenario) in TLA Food Services Ltd v 1144707 Alberta Ltd, 2011 ABQB 550, distilling the following principles: 1. When a defendant is noted in default, it is deemed to have admitted the allegations in the Statement of Claim; 2. Before granting default judgment the Court must still inquire as to whether a cause of action is made out in the Statement of Claim, and may direct a hearing on the matter; 3. A defendant who has been noted in default cannot adduce evidence to contradict the facts alleged in the Statement of Claim in the course of a hearing for the assessment of damages; 4. Quantum of damages may be assessed based on affidavit evidence; 5. R. 152 of the previous rules gives the Chambers judge discretion as to whether to grant default judgment ex parte based on affidavit evidence or to require that notice be given and an assessment set down for hearing. [para 24] [emphasis added] [76] For reference, here is former R. 152: If a sole defendant has, or all the defendants have, been noted in default, the plaintiff may: a. apply ex parte to the court for judgment, and the judge hearing the application may i. upon proof of the plaintiff's claim by affidavit or otherwise, give final judgment or direct an accounting, [or] ii. set the matter over for a hearing on notice, and notice shall be given to a defendant in the same manner as hereinafter provided on assessment or b. set the matter down for assessment, giving at least 10 days notice of the date set for the assessment. [77] Justice Shelley's distillation has been found applicable in the new (2010) Rules era, as reflected by its endorsement in Smith (ABCA — cited above) and other decisions, including Lund v Quinn Maintenance Inc, 2020 ABQB 722 (Eamon J) (para 8); Simmer v Copithorne, 2018 ABQB 525 (Eamon J.) (para 6); Roberts v Safadi, 2018 ABQB 165 (Mandziuk J.) (para 8); and Argent v Gray, 2015 ABQB 292 (Dario J.) (para 45).

BOOK_C.title: Application for judgment against defendant noted in default
BOOK_C.division_heading: Division 3 – ACTIONS STARTED BY STATEMENT OF CLAIM
BOOK_C.operative_text_raw:
(1) The plaintiff may, without notice to any other party, on proof of the plaintiff’s claim, apply to the Court for judgment in respect of a claim for which default judgment has not been entered if (a) one or more defendants are noted in default, or (b) the defendant’s statement of defence is struck out.
(2) In the circumstances described in subrule (1) the plaintiff is entitled to a costs award.
(3) The Court may do one or more of the following:
